justification: Fresh read of the whole article, then a fresh WebFetch of both round-1 comparison pages to re-confirm they are still the class of result this query surfaces. GeeksforGeeks gives a five-step 'assign constant cost, count operations, take worst case, drop constants' recipe with one nested-loop worked example and a table that name-drops 'recursion and backtracking' complexities without deriving any of them; it names neither recurrence relations nor the Master Theorem and verifies nothing by execution. freeCodeCamp is a single linear-vs-binary-search comparison with manual counting, no procedure, no recursion, no recurrence relations, no Master Theorem, no code execution. This article covers five loop shapes (sequential, independent-nested, dependent-inner-bound, multiply/divide), recursion trees, the substitution method, a correctly-stated and fully-derived three-case Master Theorem, and three named exceptions to it (subtract-not-divide, unequal subproblems, the gap between cases) -- every derivation backed by an instrumented C# program whose counters match the algebra exactly, plus four non-trivial worked exercises with solutions. That is a different class of resource than either comparison page, and would have scored 9-9.5 in round 1 had it not been capped by a factual error. This round verifies the writer's three fixes. (1) The dotnet callout: I independently instrumented both functions (root at depth 0) rather than trusting the article's numbers. RecursiveMax on n=256 gives calls=511 (matching the article's 2n-1 row) and maxDepth=8, confirming the article's corrected claim that its stack never exceeds Theta(log n) frames even though its call count is Theta(n) -- this now agrees with, rather than contradicts, the article's own earlier statement that halving 'describes how deep the recursion goes... not how many calls happen in total.' The replacement example, first-element-pivot quicksort on already-sorted input (T(n) = T(n-1) + Theta(n)), measured maxDepth=255 for n=256 in my own harness, exactly matching the article's claim of '255 levels deep for 256 elements' -- correct, since T(n)=T(n-1)+Theta(n) peels off exactly one element per call, one recursive call per level, all the way to the base case. The fix is not just non-contradictory, it is numerically verified. (2) CLRS chapter 7 is now cited inline ('the degenerate case CLRS chapter 7 walks through for exactly this pivot choice') at the exact sentence describing the sorted-input worst case, resolving the round-1 major finding that a listed source was never cited in the body. (3) The '1 megabyte' default-stack-size claim is now hyperlinked to the Thread(ThreadStart, Int32) constructor page at the point the claim is made; I re-fetched that page myself and confirmed it states, under .NET Framework 4 and later, 'only fully trusted code can set maxStackSize to a value that is greater than the default stack size (1 megabyte)' -- the citation is accurate and now inline, matching how every other cited fact on the page is linked. (4) The Karatsuba claim is honestly softened, not just hedged: round 1's text asserted 'it is the cost of Karatsuba's integer multiplication algorithm, which splits an n-digit multiplication into three multiplications of n/2 digits... beating the naive O(n^2) method for large enough n' -- a specific, named, sourced-sounding claim with no citation behind it. The new text drops the name and the unverifiable performance-crossover claim, and describes only the well-known, uncontroversial shape of the technique ('combine three half-size multiplications with extra additions instead'), which is exactly the kind of fact the brief's own carve-out for un-openable textbooks permits without a page citation. It reads as an honest description of a real technique's shape, not an attributed factual claim standing on nothing. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion.md` passes clean from PowerShell: 'PASS complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion.md blocks=25 executed=12'. I re-derived the remaining recurrences by hand as an independent check, not just a re-read of round 1's derivations: the merge recurrence's exact n*log2(n) moves (case 2, ratio 1.00 at every power-of-two row); the cross-pairs case-3 regularity check (a*f(n/b) = n^2/8 = c*f(n) with c=1/2, satisfying c<1 at the boundary); the triple-split exercise's ratio converging to 2^log2(3) = 3.00 from above; and the gap-case recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+O(log n), which satisfies none of the three cases and whose recursion-tree sum gives Theta((log n)^2), matching the L(L+1)/2 table exactly. No new factual, sourcing or code errors were introduced by the round-2 edits, and none of the un-touched material contains an error I could find. The remaining distance to a 10 is not any specific defect -- it is that a 10 is reserved for something no stronger existing page on the query touches at all; this article is clearly better than both pages actually ranking for the query today, which is what the 9.4 reflects.
